children: An allusion to Richard III’s cry “A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!” in Richard III, Act V.
Also an allusion to Genesis 25-27, the rivalry between Issac’s elder son Esau and his younger son, Jacob, who cheats Esau.
Once, when Esau is exhausted from a hunting trip, he sells his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew.
Later, when Issac is blind and on his deathbed, Jacob disguises himself as Esau and tricks Issac into giving Jacob a blessing meant for Esau. Jacob’s voice is his only tell. Gen 27:22 reads:
“Jacob went close to his father Isaac, who touched him and said, ‘The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.’ ”
Esau arrives too late and is distraught. Verse 34: “When Esau heard his father’s words, he burst out with a loud and bitter cry and said to his father, ‘Bless me—me too, my father!’ ”

Stephen’s comparison of his voice with Esau’s voice in the context of brothers and fathers in conflict is complex. Does he feel wronged by his younger brother as Esau was by Jacob, as he argues Shakespeare was by his younger brothers?
